```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

game_films_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-06-09/game_films.csv"
)
```

## Introduction

This project uses the "Films Based on Video Games" dataset, compiled from a Wikipedia list and published on TidyTuesday on the 9th of June 2026. It has `r nrow(game_films_raw)` films and `r ncol(game_films_raw)` columns, and each row is one film (theatrical, direct-to-video, television, short or documentary). Many budget, box office and score values are missing, so we focus mostly on theatrical releases. Our team chose it because video game adaptations are popular and often criticized, and we wanted to see whether they make money and how critics and audiences react.

We answer two questions. Question 1 asks whether films with bigger budgets earn a better return on investment (ROI), using `budget_low` and `budget_high` (the lowest and highest estimates for budget) and `worldwide_box_office` (total worldwide earnings). The currency columns `budget_currency` and `worldwide_box_office_currency` give the currency symbol of each amount and the column `release_date` allows us to convert all monetary values into USD of today's worth. Question 2 asks whether critics and audiences agree and whether the gap changes over time. To answer this question, we use `rotten_tomatoes` (percent of positive critic reviews), `metacritic` (critic score out of 100), `cinema_score` (audience letter grade from A+ to F) and `release_date`.


## Question 1: Do Bigger Budgets Earn a Better Return?

### Introduction

Do films based on video games earn a better return on investment (ROI) when they have bigger budgets, or do low and medium budget films do better? We define ROI as `(worldwide box office - budget) / budget`, so an ROI of 1 means the film earned a profit equal to its whole budget, and a negative ROI means it lost money. To answer this we use `budget_low` and `budget_high`, `worldwide_box_office`, the two currency columns, `release_date`, and an OECD consumer price index (CPI) table that allows us to convert money in today's value.

We are interested in this because box office totals make expensive films look best by default, while ROI shows how much a film earned compared to what was risked. This matters for anyone deciding how much to spend on a new game adaptation.

### Approach

We split the films into three budget groups (low, medium and high), each group has about the same number of films so we do not have to choose arbitrary dollar cutoffs. We chose a boxplot of ROI by group, with the boxes colored by group, because it shows the median and the spread of each group, and a few huge hits do not distort it the way they would distort an average (Healy 2018, Ch. 4). Each film is also drawn as a dot, so the distribution stays visible. A label prints the median ROI of each group so the groups can be compared directly.

Our second plot is a scatterplot of each film's budget against its worldwide box office, both on log scales and colored by budget group. A scatterplot is the right choice because it uses every film's exact budget instead of cutting budget into groups, so we can check that the boxplot result does not depend on where the group boundaries fall (Healy 2018, Ch. 3). The log scales keep a $3 million film and a $250 million film readable on the same axes. A dashed line marks where box office equals budget, so a film above the line earned more than it cost and its distance from the line reflects its ROI. The two plots are of different types, and both use color to show the budget groups.

### Analysis

```{r}
#| label: q1-data

# Step 1: Load the inflation (CPI) table and keep only the consumer price index (CPI) values
CPI_raw <- readr::read_csv('00_raw_data/OECD_Table.csv')
CPI <- CPI_raw |>
  filter(UNIT_MEASURE == "IX") |>
  select(REF_AREA,TIME_PERIOD,OBS_VALUE,OBS_VALUE_TODAY)

# Step 2: Create a Lookup table: currency symbol -> country code and exchange rate to USD
currency_country <- tibble(
  budget_currency = c("$", "¥", "£"),
  worldwide_box_office_currency = c("$", "¥", "£"),
  country_code = c("USA", "JPN", "GBR"),
  exchange_rate = c(1,0.0063,1.32))

# Step 3: Budget in today's value in USD (midpoint of low and high, adjusted with the CPI)
game_films_budget <- game_films_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(budget_currency)) |>
  mutate(
    #Take the budget as the midpoint between the low and high estimates
    budget_estimate = (budget_low+budget_high)/2,
    release_year = as.double(format(release_date,"%Y")))

#Join the lookup table 
game_films_budget <- left_join(
  game_films_budget,
  currency_country,
  by="budget_currency")

#Join the CPI table
game_films_budget <- left_join(
  game_films_budget,
  CPI,
  by=c(
    "country_code"="REF_AREA",
    "release_year"="TIME_PERIOD"
    ))

# The budget in today's value becomes the original amount times (the current CPI divided by the past CPI)
# To convert to USD multiply by the exchange rate
game_films_budget <- game_films_budget |>
  mutate(
    budget_estimate_today = budget_estimate*(OBS_VALUE_TODAY/OBS_VALUE),
    budget_estimate_today_usd = budget_estimate_today*exchange_rate)

# Step 4: Box office in today's value in USD (same steps as the budget)
game_films_box_office <- game_films_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(worldwide_box_office_currency)) |>
  mutate(release_year = as.double(format(release_date,"%Y")))

game_films_box_office <- left_join(
  game_films_box_office,
  currency_country,
  by="worldwide_box_office_currency")

game_films_box_office <- left_join(
  game_films_box_office,
  CPI,
  by=c(
    "country_code"="REF_AREA",
    "release_year"="TIME_PERIOD"
  ))

game_films_box_office <- game_films_box_office |>
  mutate(
    worldwide_box_office_today = worldwide_box_office*(OBS_VALUE_TODAY/OBS_VALUE),
    worldwide_box_office_today_usd = worldwide_box_office_today*exchange_rate)

# Step 5: Join budget and box office (only films that have both), then compute ROI
game_films <- inner_join(
  game_films_budget,
  game_films_box_office,
  by=c("title","director","release_date"))

game_films <- game_films |>
  select(category.x:release_date,original_game_publisher.x,budget_estimate_today_usd,worldwide_box_office_today_usd) |>
  mutate(ROI = (worldwide_box_office_today_usd-budget_estimate_today_usd)/budget_estimate_today_usd) 

# Step 6: Split budget into three groups with about the same number of films
budget_cutoff <- quantile(
  game_films$budget_estimate_today_usd,
  probs = c(0,1/3,2/3,1))

game_films$budget_group <- cut(game_films$budget_estimate_today_usd,breaks=budget_cutoff,labels=c("Low\n$3-46M","Medium\n$46-92M","High\n$92-259M"),include.lowest=TRUE)

# Step 7: Summary numbers per budget group (used in the plot label and the discussion)
group_summary <- game_films |>
  group_by(budget_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_ROI = median(ROI), pct_loss = mean(ROI < 0))
```

```{r}
#| label: q1-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "ROI by budget group"
game_films %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = budget_group, y = ROI, fill = budget_group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = dplyr::filter(game_films, ROI > 10), aes(label = title),
            nudge_x = 0.22, hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_label(data = group_summary,
             aes(x = budget_group, y = 0.3 * max(game_films$ROI),
                 label = sprintf("Median ROI: %.1fx", median_ROI)),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "white", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1.4))) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 10, labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "x")) +
  labs(
    title = "Low-budget films have the biggest hits, but not a higher typical ROI",
    subtitle = "ROI = (worldwide box office - budget) / budget",
    x = "Budget group (inflation-adjusted, today's USD)",
    y = "Return on investment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| label: q1-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Budget vs worldwide box office (log scales)"
ggplot(game_films, aes(x = budget_estimate_today_usd / 1e6,
                       y = worldwide_box_office_today_usd / 1e6,
                       color = budget_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "M", accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "M", accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", labels = function(x) gsub("\n", " ", x)) +
  labs(
    title = "Bigger budgets earn bigger grosses",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: worldwide box office equals budget",
    x = "Production budget (log scale)",
    y = "Worldwide box office (log scale)",
    color = "Budget tier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Discussion

The median ROI rises with budget: `r sprintf("%.2f", group_summary$median_ROI[1])` for low (`r group_summary$n[1]` films), `r sprintf("%.2f", group_summary$median_ROI[2])` for medium (`r group_summary$n[2]` films) and `r sprintf("%.2f", group_summary$median_ROI[3])` for high (`r group_summary$n[3]` films), so bigger-budget films yielded higher returns, which is the opposite of what we expected. The low group is the least predictable. `r round(100 * group_summary$pct_loss[1])`% of its films lost money, yet it also has the biggest hit, with an ROI of `r sprintf("%.1f", max(game_films$ROI))`, because a cheap film needs only a small box office for a large ROI. Furthermore, the boxes overlap a lot, so the differences between groups are small.

Figure 2 shows the same pattern in absolute terms: box office tends to rise with budget, but the points scatter widely around the dashed break-even line, and `r sum(game_films$ROI < 0)` of the `r nrow(game_films)` films ended below it. The three biggest sucesses, *Pokémon: The First Movie*, *Iron Lung* and *Five Nights at Freddy's*, all have low budgets, and we think this is because each already had a large following. Two of the movies have well known franchises and the movie *Iron Lung* was directed by a well-known YouTuber (Markiplier). A cheap film generally cannot create that audience, so low-budget ROI looks more like a lottery that a few franchise films win. High-budget films mostly sit within a few times their budget, so their returns are steadier than those of low-budget films.

A few extreme hits stretch the y-axis of Figure 1, which makes the boxes harder to compare, so we label them by name. The results cover only `r nrow(game_films)` theatrical films, and we did not look at genre. Budgets are estimates that do not include marketing, and box office is gross ticket sales, not profit, so an ROI near zero likely means a loss. Our conclusions are descriptive and show that while higher budgets generally lead to higher returns, there are some low budget movies which do exceptionally well. 

## Question 2: Do Critics and Audiences Agree on Video Game Films?

### Introduction

Do critics and audiences agree about films based on video games, and has the gap changed over time? Critics are represented by `rotten_tomatoes` (the Rotten Tomatoes critic score, the percent of positive reviews) and `metacritic` (a weighted average of critic scores out of 100). Audiences are represented by `cinema_score`, the letter grade (A+ to F) given by audiences polled on opening weekend, and we use `release_date` to place each film in time. The dataset has no Rotten Tomatoes audience score, so CinemaScore is our only audience measure, and it has to be converted from letters to points before it can be compared with the critic scores.

We are interested in this because video game films often seem to be liked by fans and disliked by reviewers, and a studio would want to know whether that pattern is real and whether it is fading. We define the gap as the audience score minus the critic score, where the critic score is the average of the Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic scores. A positive gap means audiences rated the film higher than critics did. Only some (51) theatrical films have all three ratings, so this analysis covers a small, better-known subset of releases.

### Approach

Our first plot is a scatterplot of the gap against release date with a fitted linear trend line. A scatterplot shows every film as a point, so we can see the spread of the gap and spot unusual films, and the trend line summarizes whether the gap is rising, falling or flat (Healy 2018, Ch. 3). The points are colored by the budget group from Question 1 to check whether expensive or cheap films behave differently. We did not use yearly averages because there are too few films per year for them to be reliable.

Our second plot compares critics and audiences by era (before 2010, the 2010s and the 2020s). For each era it shows the average critic score and the average audience score as two colored dots joined by a line, so the length of the line is the gap. This dumbbell plot is the clearest way to show how far apart two scores are, and it also shows whether the gap shrinks because one group moves or both do. The eras are only a way to get groups of 15 to 21 films, so the cutoffs are our choice. The two plots are of different types, and both use color.

### Analysis

The first block converts CinemaScore letter grades into numerical scores on a 100-point scale. Each letter grade corresponds to a 10-point range, with grades within each range separated by 3 points, from A+ (100) to F− (54 and computes the gap. This is the same rating as used in this course. Missing and "N/A" grades stay missing, so only films with all three ratings and a release date are kept. It also adds the budget group from Question 1, creates the eras, and computes the numbers used in the discussion.

```{r}
#| label: q2-data
grades <- c("A+" = 100, "A" = 97, "A-" = 94,
            "B+" = 90,  "B" = 87, "B-" = 84,
            "C+" = 80,  "C" = 77, "C-" = 74,
            "D+" = 70,  "D" = 67, "D-" = 64,
            "F+" = 60,  "F" = 57, "F-" = 54)

q2 <- game_films_raw |>
  mutate(
    audience = unname(grades[cinema_score]),   # "N/A" and NA become NA
    critic   = (rotten_tomatoes + metacritic) / 2,
    gap      = audience - critic,
    year     = as.numeric(format(release_date, "%Y"))
  ) |>
  # budget group comes from the Question 1 table
  left_join(select(game_films, title, director, release_date, budget_group),
            by = c("title", "director", "release_date")) |>
  filter(!is.na(gap), !is.na(release_date)) |>
  mutate(era = cut(year, breaks = c(-Inf, 2009, 2019, Inf),
                   labels = c("Before 2010", "2010s", "2020s")))

# Average scores and gap per era (used in the second plot and the discussion)
era_summary <- q2 |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_gap = mean(gap),
            mean_critic = mean(critic), mean_audience = mean(audience)) |>
  mutate(era_label = factor(paste0(era, "\n(n = ", n, ")"),
                            levels = paste0(era, "\n(n = ", n, ")")))

# Linear trend of the gap over time (used in the discussion)
trend <- lm(gap ~ year, data = q2)
rho2  <- cor.test(q2$year, q2$gap, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

Figure 3 shows the gap for each film over time, colored by budget group, with a linear trend line.

```{r}
#| label: q2-gap-over-time
#| fig-cap: "Audience minus critic score over time"
ggplot(q2, aes(x = release_date, y = gap)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "grey30",se=FALSE, fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(color = budget_group), size = 2.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", na.value = "grey60",
                     labels = function(x) gsub("\n", " ", x)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 80)) +
  labs(
    title = "Audiences rate game films higher than critics, but the gap is shrinking",
    subtitle = "Above 0 means the audience score is higher than the critic score",
    x = "Release date",
    y = "Audience minus critics (points)",
    color = "Budget group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Figure 4 shows the average critic and audience scores in each era. The line between the dots is the gap.

```{r}
#| label: q2-era
#| fig-cap: "Average critic and audience scores by era"
cols <- c("Critics" = "#D55E00", "Audience" = "#0072B2")

ggplot(era_summary, aes(y = era_label)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = mean_critic, xend = mean_audience, yend = era_label),
               color = "grey60", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean_critic,   color = "Critics"),  size = 4.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean_audience, color = "Audience"), size = 4.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (mean_critic + mean_audience) / 2,
                label = sprintf("gap %.0f", mean_gap)), vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(
    title = "Critics are catching up with audiences, but a large gap remains",
    x = "Average score (0-100)", y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Discussion

All `r nrow(q2)` films have a positive gap, meaning audiences rated every film higher than critics did. This may partly reflect our conversion of letter grades into numerical scores, which restricts ratings to values between 54 and 100. Converting a more granular scale into a less granular one introduces potential bias, as differences between ratings may be distorted by the conversion. However, since our analysis focuses on changes in the gap over time rather than its absolute magnitude, this limitation is less important for our question. The trend line in Figure 3 slopes downward by about `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(coef(trend)["year"]))` points per year (p = `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(trend)$coefficients["year", 4])`; Spearman's rho = `r sprintf("%.2f", unname(rho2$estimate))`), so the gap has narrowed over time even though it is still large for recent films. The scatter around the line is wide, and no budget group stands out, so the trend describes the typical film and not any single one.

Figure 4 shows why the gap narrows. The average critic score rises from `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_critic[1])` before 2010 to `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_critic[2])` in the 2010s and `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_critic[3])` in the 2020s, while the average audience score only moves from `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_audience[1])` to `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_audience[3])`, so the gap falls from `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_gap[1])` to `r sprintf("%.0f", era_summary$mean_gap[3])` points. We think critics became kinder to recent adaptations, while audiences were already giving high grades to films that critics disliked, such as *Mortal Kombat Annihilation* and the early *Pokémon* films. A likely reason is that CinemaScore polls opening-weekend audiences, who are self-selected fans that came to see characters they already like.

Two limitations matter. First, the gap partly reflects the measurement scales: CinemaScore grades cluster near the top and may be inflated by fans, while Rotten Tomatoes is the percent of positive reviews, so a positive gap is expected even if both groups felt the same way. The conversion of letter grades to points is also a judgment call, so the size of the gap is best read as a comparison across films and eras. Second, only `r nrow(q2)` films have all three ratings, CinemaScore mainly covers wide U.S. releases, and the era groups are small, so the trend may not hold for the rest of the data.
